summary:
Vaziri frames go-to-market orchestration as describing a motion — a campaign, playbook, or experiment — and having it automatically distributed across outbound, paid ads, web, and in-app channels. His running example, offering Pro V1 golf balls to East Coast construction company golfers, requires building an audience, generating copy and creative, and producing in-app nudges from a single intent statement. He identifies three bottlenecks: inconsistent data across systems, reps buried in operational busywork, and the months-long coordination cost of writing proposals and convincing teams to adopt new playbooks. Agents, combined with a consistent data foundation, are what make execution close to the operator's point of action feasible.

Ramp's foundation is an internal customer data platform unifying CRM, product, enrichment, web, and buying signals with interaction data. Real-time events flow onto Kafka and into Postgres, preserving referential integrity across entities. Unstructured data — call transcripts, emails, notes, enablement materials — is chunked, embedded, and stored so agents can search a scoped subset rather than loading the full corpus into context. Offline batch compute via DBT and Snowflake is reverse-ETL'd back into the same layer.

Ramp's tactic is to solve for one team first, then scale sideways. Account managers were the first target via pre-meeting briefs aggregating usage, vitals, agenda, and open tickets. A sneaky hard prerequisite — mapping attendee emails back to accounts when one person represents multiple businesses — is solved once and persisted. Every brief run is a durable Temporal thread where each tool and model call is an activity, so workers resume rather than reprocess.

A skill library lets teams define their own brief format, which is what drove adoption. Every night, agents fan out per account, using CDP access, vector search, system-level meeting prep skills, and user-supplied custom instructions to produce briefs. The same foundation extends to post-meeting follow-ups and automatic CRM updates, where transcripts are parsed, opportunities pre-filled, and a human thumbs-up completes the loop. Scaling horizontally is mainly an exercise of adding skills, data integrations, and ingestion — for AEs the emphasis shifts toward third-party data and pre-sales context. Ramp also built a GT MCP that exposes the same tools and skills to employees, federating capabilities to people building their own agents and vibe-coded applications, whose prompts and skills feed back into productionized use cases.

takeaways: Go-to-market orchestration means describing a motion and letting systems distribute it across outbound, ads, web, and in-app channels.
Three bottlenecks block GTM execution: inconsistent data, rep busywork, and the months-long cost of coordinating playbooks across teams.
Ramp built an internal customer data platform combining CRM, product, enrichment, web, and buying signals on Postgres + Kafka, with unstructured data embedded for scoped search.
Solve for one team first (account managers with pre-meeting briefs), then mirror patterns sideways by adding skills, integrations, and ingestion.
Every run is a durable Temporal thread with each tool and model call as an activity, enabling resume rather than reprocess on worker failure.
A skill library that lets teams define their own brief format, plus custom instructions, is what drove adoption.
The GT MCP federates the same tools and skills to employees, turning their vibe-coded agents into a feedback loop that feeds productionized use cases.
Pre-meeting briefs scale into post-meeting follow-ups and automatic CRM updates with a human-in-the-loop thumbs-up.

sections.title: What go-to-market orchestration means
sections.summary: Vaziri defines orchestration as describing a motion (campaign, playbook, experiment) and automating its distribution across outbound, ads, web, and in-app channels. He introduces the Pro V1 golf balls for East Coast construction golfers example and lists three bottlenecks: inconsistent data, rep busywork, and the months-long coordination cost of adopting playbooks. Agents plus a consistent data substrate are what make near-point-of-execution automation possible.

sections.title: Building an internal customer data platform
sections.summary: Ramp built an internal CDP unifying CRM, product, enrichment, web, and buying signals with interaction data. Real-time events flow onto Kafka and into Postgres to maintain referential integrity across entities. Unstructured data (calls, emails, notes, enablement) is chunked and embedded so agents can search scoped subsets. Offline batch compute via DBT and Snowflake is reverse-ETL'd into the same layer.

sections.title: Solve one team, then scale sideways
sections.summary: Ramp's tactic is to identify overlapping workflows across teams, ship for one team first, and mirror patterns to others. The first target is account managers, via pre-meeting briefs that aggregate usage, vitals, agenda, and open tickets so AMs can walk into back-to-back meetings prepared.

sections.title: Pre-meeting briefs and durable Temporal threads
sections.summary: Building briefs requires mapping attendee emails back to accounts — a sneaky hard problem when one person represents multiple businesses — and persisting that mapping for downstream consumers. Each run is a durable Temporal thread where every tool call and model call is an activity, so a worker that dies resumes from accumulated state instead of reprocessing. Temporal also provides config-scoped tools and human-in-the-loop pauses.

sections.title: Skill library for unstructured data
sections.summary: Unstructured data — meeting transcripts, emails, enablement, playbooks — is the most valuable artifact and is chunked, embedded, and stored in Turbo Buffer for vector, attribute, and keyword search scoped to a specific account. This avoids loading the full corpus into agent context.

sections.title: Operational background agents
sections.summary: A skill library lets teams define their own brief format and supply custom instructions, which is what drove adoption. Every night, agents fan out per account to compute meeting prep using CDP access, vector search, system-level skills, and user custom instructions. The same foundation extends to post-meeting follow-ups and automatic CRM updates that pre-fill opportunities from transcripts and request a human thumbs-up.

sections.title: Scaling horizontally and the GT MCP
sections.summary: Scaling to other teams is mainly an exercise of creating skills, data integrations, and ingestion — for AEs the focus shifts to third-party data and pre-sales context. Ramp built a GT MCP that exposes the same tools and skills used by background agents to employees, federating capabilities to people who build their own agents and vibe-coded applications. Their prompts and skills feed back into productionized use cases, turning employees into a discovery and productization loop.

sections.title: Back to the golf balls — multi-channel distribution
sections.summary: Vaziri returns to the Pro V1 golf example to show that these vertical builds are the foundation for multi-team, multi-channel distribution. Funneling intent into Ramp Revenue means creating SDR audiences, generating personalized copy and sequences, spinning up landing pages and creative, and routing artifacts for review. Agents hold context across multiple campaign options to balance exploration versus known returns, with guardrails for compliance, rules of engagement, and context awareness.

sections.title: Q&A — advice for smaller teams
sections.summary: For a smaller company, Vaziri recommends finding specific use cases to automate and solving narrow problems first rather than spending a year designing a perfect architecture. He recalls that three years ago it was two people using GPT 3.5 for automated outbound — piecing together vertical solutions and connecting them over time is how Ramp itself started.

demonstrations: Pre-meeting briefs for account managers that aggregate usage, vitals, agenda, and open tickets.
Durable Temporal threads where each tool call and model call is an activity.
Embedding and chunking of unstructured sales data for scoped agent search.
Offline batch compute via DBT and Snowflake reverse-ETL'd back into the operational layer.
Nightly fan-out of background agents per account to compute meeting prep using CDP, vector DB, system skills, and user custom instructions.
Post-meeting follow-ups and automatic CRM updates that pre-fill opportunities from transcripts and request a human thumbs-up.
GT MCP exposing the same tools and skills to employees who build their own agents and vibe-coded applications.
limitations: Designing the perfect architecture is not realistic; build narrow automations first.
Sales teams are in back-to-back meetings all day, leaving little time for operational work.
Agents must understand the full breadth of company context to be effective.
Scaling horizontally to new teams requires new skills, integrations, and ingestion work.
quantitativeClaims: Ramp's addressable market is 'pretty much like the entire US' and now expanding internationally.
Coordination cost operates on 'the order of like months' rather than weeks.
Three years ago Ramp had only two people building automated outbound with GPT 3.5.
